claims.text: Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys is governed by the dynamic stability and rapid reformation of the passive oxide film.
Increasing Cr or Al content produces a denser, more adherent, and self-healing protective oxide layer.
AlCoCrFeNi can have a single-phase FCC/BCC structure.
AlCoCrFeNi forms a thin passive oxide film under oxidizing conditions.
Increasing Cr and/or Al will promote formation of a more robust and rapidly reforming oxide film.
Alloy composition determines passive-film density, adhesion, and regeneration kinetics.
Mechanical loading periodically disrupts the passive film.
Enhanced passive-film-forming capability allows sufficiently rapid film reformation to inhibit local corrosion at wear sites.
Passive-film self-healing minimizes cumulative damage from both mechanical wear and chemical attack.
An alloy optimized for passive-film formation will have a lower wear rate than the baseline during combined tribocorrosion.
An alloy optimized for passive-film formation will have a lower corrosion current density than the baseline during combined tribocorrosion.
Combined degradation in the optimized alloy will be less severe than the sum of its isolated wear and isolated corrosion effects.
The protective mechanism will operate under moderate loads and corrosive conditions when passive-film regeneration can keep pace with disruption.
At very high mechanical stresses or in more aggressive chemical environments, film disruption can outpace reformation and eliminate the benefit.
Grain size and phase distribution may influence tribocorrosion outcomes.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing a baseline alloy with a Cr/Al-enhanced alloy under matched combined, wear-only, and corrosion-only conditions.
Failure to reduce both wear rate and corrosion current density, together with combined degradation equaling or exceeding the isolated-effect sum, is specified as a falsifying result.
